Stage 3 · Language

Moving something without causing a problem

The same four moves, once on the phone and once in writing.

Read these four lines from a phone call.
  • There’s been a change of plan.
  • I’m afraid I’ve got something else on tomorrow lunchtime.
  • How about getting together after work instead?
  • I’ll speak to her, then I’ll get back to you.
Which of the four is the one people most often forget?
Changing a plan costs somebody else time, and English wraps the message accordingly.

When you move a meeting or cancel an arrangement, you are asking another person to absorb the disruption. English handles this with a fixed sequence of softening moves, and leaving them out is read as carelessness rather than as efficiency.

Compare I can’t come on Thursday with I’m afraid I have to move our meeting — would it be possible to reschedule for Friday morning? Both convey the same fact. The second adds an apology marker (I’m afraid), a proposal, and crucially a question, which leaves the decision with the other person. That question form is the single most important habit in this lesson: Could we reschedule…? invites agreement, while We’ll move it to Friday issues an instruction.

A professional email has a fixed architecture that the reader expects: a greeting, a statement of why you are writing, the change itself, the proposal, the apology, and a close with a matching sign-off. Readers scan for these parts; an email that omits one of them takes longer to process and generates a reply asking for it.

Register is the other half of the skill, and it must be consistent from the greeting to the sign-off. I am writing to inform you… followed by Anyway, see you then! is the commonest failure in B1 written work. One further convention worth knowing before you write: Yours sincerely pairs with a named greeting, and Yours faithfully with Dear Sir or Madam.

Before you look at the table: the table below sets out the email skeleton in order, with the phrases that fill each slot. Read it as a sequence — the order of the parts is what makes the message easy to answer.
The four moves, spoken and written
The moveOn the phoneIn an email
Announce itThere’s been a change of plan.Unfortunately there has been a change of plan.
Give the reasonI’m afraid I’ve got something else on. · I’m supposed to be…I’m afraid I have to attend…
Suggest a new timeHow about …ing instead? · Are you free on Thursday?Would it be possible to reschedule for…? · Could we reschedule…?
Say what happens nextI’ll get back to you. · I’ll speak to her and let you know.I will confirm as soon as I hear. · Apologies for any inconvenience.
If you cannot make itI’m really sorry, but I can’t make it then.I am afraid I am not available then.

The reason comes before the request. Say why first, then ask. A request with no reason sounds like an instruction, and a reason with no request leaves the other person to do the work.

Be supposed to is the everyday way of saying “this is the plan, but…” I’m supposed to be playing tennis tells the listener at once that you are willing to move it.

The mistake to avoid. Do not apologise three times. In English, once is polite and three times sounds like something serious has happened. One I’m really sorry, or one Apologies for any inconvenience at the end. Not both, and not more.

Sign-offs. Best regards and Kind regards are safe with anybody at work. Yours faithfully and Yours sincerely recycled from Lesson 12 belong in a first, formal letter, not in an email to a colleague you know.

Full grammar reference — changing arrangements, and the professional email

What it is

The functional language of rearranging: announcing that something has changed, proposing an alternative, apologising for the inconvenience, and confirming the new plan. Alongside it sits the fixed architecture of a professional email — greeting, reason for writing, the change, the proposal, the apology, the close — and the register choices that hold it together.

What it means, and what it does

Changing a plan costs the other person time, so English wraps the message in softeners. I can’t come on Thursday is accurate but bare. I’m afraid I have to move our meeting — would it be possible to reschedule for Friday? carries the same information plus an apology, a proposal and a question that leaves control with the other person. At work, the wrapping is not politeness theatre; it is what keeps the relationship usable.

When and why we use it

When you move a meeting or cancel an arrangement, you are asking another person to absorb the disruption. English handles this with a fixed sequence of softening moves, and leaving them out is read as carelessness rather than as efficiency.

Compare I can’t come on Thursday with I’m afraid I have to move our meeting — would it be possible to reschedule for Friday morning? Both convey the same fact. The second adds an apology marker (I’m afraid), a proposal, and crucially a question, which leaves the decision with the other person. That question form is the single most important habit in this lesson: Could we reschedule…? invites agreement, while We’ll move it to Friday issues an instruction.

A professional email has a fixed architecture that the reader expects: a greeting, a statement of why you are writing, the change itself, the proposal, the apology, and a close with a matching sign-off. Readers scan for these parts; an email that omits one of them takes longer to process and generates a reply asking for it.

Register is the other half of the skill, and it must be consistent from the greeting to the sign-off. I am writing to inform you… followed by Anyway, see you then! is the commonest failure in B1 written work. One further convention worth knowing before you write: Yours sincerely pairs with a named greeting, and Yours faithfully with Dear Sir or Madam.

Typical situations

You need this for postponing meetings, cancelling appointments, warning a colleague that a deadline will slip, and any professional message where you are the one causing the inconvenience.

  • Announcing the change — the standard opener, spoken or written.There’s been a change of plan — I can’t make Thursday.
  • Softening bad news — I’m afraid before the problem.I’m afraid I have to postpone our call.
  • Proposing an alternative — a question, not a statement, so the other person can refuse.Would it be possible to move it to Friday morning?
  • Offering options — two choices are more helpful than one.Could we reschedule for either Thursday afternoon or Friday?
  • Apologising for the disruption — the fixed phrase; note the noun.Apologies for any inconvenience this may cause.
  • Confirming the new arrangement — closing the loop so nothing is left open.I’ll confirm the new time by the end of the day.
  • Signing off — matched to the greeting.Best regards, / Kind regards,

How it differs from similar structures

Could we reschedule…? (asks permission, softest) · Would it be possible to…? (formal, impersonal) · I need to move it. (statement of fact — only when you have the authority).
postpone = move to a later time · cancel = remove entirely · reschedule = move to a different time, earlier or later. They are not interchangeable, and choosing wrongly changes what you have told your colleague.

How to build it

Announce: There’s been a change of plan / I’m afraid I have to + base verb
Propose: Would it be possible to + base verb?  ·  Could we + base verb?
Apologise: Apologies for + noun / verb-ing  ·  I’m sorry for + verb-ing
Email skeleton: greeting → reason for writing → the change → the proposal → the apology → close + sign-off
Greeting — formalDear Ms Iskakova, — surname, comma, and never Dear Mrs unless you know.
Greeting — neutralDear Aigul, · Hello Aigul,
Reason for writingI’m writing to let you know that… · I’m writing regarding…
The changeI’m afraid I have to… · Unfortunately, something has come up and…
The proposalWould it be possible to…? · Could we reschedule for…? · Would Friday suit you?
The apologyApologies for any inconvenience. · Sorry for the short notice.
CloseI look forward to hearing from you. · Thanks for your understanding.
Sign-offBest regards, / Kind regards, (neutral–formal) · Yours sincerely, (named person) · Yours faithfully, (Dear Sir/Madam)

Usage notes and exceptions

  • The proposal should be a question, not an instruction. Could we move it to Friday? leaves the decision open; We’ll move it to Friday does not, and reads as high-handed unless you outrank the reader.
  • Apologies for takes a noun or an -ing form: apologies for the delay, apologies for changing the date — never apologies to change.
  • Yours sincerely pairs with a named greeting (Dear Mr Bekov); Yours faithfully pairs with Dear Sir or Madam. Mixing them is a classic register error in exams.
  • Contractions (I’m, can’t, we’ll) are fine in neutral professional email and normal in speech. In a formal letter, write them out.
  • Keep one register throughout. I am writing to inform you… Anyway, see you then! is the commonest failure in B1 written work.
  • State the new proposal with a specific time. Could we meet later in the week? creates another round of email; Would Friday at ten suit you? ends it.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I write to inform you that the meeting is moved. → I’m writing to let you know that the meeting has been moved.Use the present continuous for the act of writing, and the perfect for the change.
  • Apologies for to change the date. → Apologies for changing the date.Apologies for takes a noun or -ing.
  • Would it be possible moving it to Friday? → Would it be possible to move it to Friday?Possible to + base verb.
  • Dear Mr Bekov, … Yours faithfully, → Dear Mr Bekov, … Yours sincerely,Faithfully goes with Dear Sir or Madam only.
  • I am afraid that I must to cancel. → I’m afraid I have to cancel.Must takes no to, and have to is more natural here.
  • Sorry for the inconveniences. → Apologies for any inconvenience.Inconvenience is uncountable in this phrase.

More examples in context

  • announcingThere’s been a change of plan — the client has moved our review.
  • softeningI’m afraid I have to pull out of Thursday’s session.
  • reason for writingI’m writing to let you know that I won’t be able to attend on Wednesday.
  • proposingWould it be possible to push it back by an hour?
  • offering optionsCould we reschedule for Thursday at four or Friday morning?
  • checkingWould Friday at ten suit you?
  • apologisingApologies for any inconvenience — I know this is short notice.
  • confirmingI’ll confirm the new time as soon as I hear from the client.
  • closingThanks for your understanding.
  • sign-offBest regards,
    Sara

A tip for remembering it

Write every rearranging message in five short moves and do not skip any of them: 1 what has changed, 2 why (one clause is enough), 3 what you propose, with a specific time, 4 the apology, 5 what happens next. Then read it once for register: if the greeting is formal, every sentence must be.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Announce the change with There’s been a change of plan or I’m afraid I have to…
  2. Make the alternative a question: Would it be possible to…? / Could we reschedule for…?
  3. Propose a specific time, not a vague one.
  4. Apologies for + noun or -ing.
  5. Yours sincerely with a name; Yours faithfully with Dear Sir or Madam.
  6. Hold one register from greeting to sign-off.

Stage 5 · Main input

The same call, written down

Read it as a writer. You are going to write one like it.

Before you read: what makes somebody agree to move a meeting without minding?

Choose one. The model does three of these and deliberately avoids one.

Subject: Thursday’s meeting — change of time

Dear Ms Aliyeva,

I am writing about our meeting on Thursday at eleven. Unfortunately there has been a change of plan: I have been asked to attend a client presentation that morning, and I am afraid I cannot move it.

Would it be possible to reschedule for later the same day? I am free from two o’clock onwards, and Friday morning would also work if that suits you better.

I have already spoken to Marat, who has confirmed that either time is fine for him. I will bring the figures we discussed, so we should still be able to finish within an hour.

Apologies for any inconvenience.

Kind regards,
Aigerim

What the model does, in five moves
  • Names the meeting first, so the reader knows what this is about before anything else.
  • Gives the change and the reason together, in one sentence.
  • Offers two new times without waiting to be asked.
  • Says what has already been sorted out — that is what makes people say yes.
  • Apologises once, then signs off. Not three times.
